items.stem: Which is the definition of gravitational field strength at a point?
options: the gravitational force per unit mass on a small mass placed at the point
the acceleration of any object at the point when thrown
the force between two unit masses 1 m apart
the work done per unit mass bringing a mass from infinity
items.answer: the gravitational force per unit mass on a small mass placed at the point
items.markingKey: g = F/m.

items.stem: Explain why the gravitational field near the Earth's surface can be treated as uniform in a laboratory but not for a satellite in orbit.
items.answer: Over a few metres the change in distance from the Earth's centre is tiny compared with the Earth's radius, so g is almost constant and lines are effectively parallel; a satellite's orbit covers distances comparable with R, so g varies significantly (radial field).
items.markingKey: height change ≪ R so g constant [1]; orbit distance comparable to R, field radial / varies [1] [2]

items.stem: Show that the units N kg⁻¹ and m s⁻² are equivalent.
items.answer: 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², so N kg⁻¹ = kg m s⁻² kg⁻¹ = m s⁻².
items.markingKey: N = kg m s⁻² [1]; cancel kg [1] [2]

items.stem: The gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars is 3.73 N kg⁻¹. An instrument package has a mass of 60 kg. Determine the weight of an instrument package on Mars.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 60 × 3.73 = 224 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A rover has a weight of 4440 N on the surface of Mercury, where it has mass 1200 kg. Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Mercury and the weight of the same object on Earth.

A lander of mass 150 kg rests on the surface of Mercury, where the gravitational field strength is 3.70 N kg⁻¹. (a) Describe the field lines close to the surface over the landing site. (b) The lander's thrusters give an upward force of 830 N on lift-off. Calculate its initial acceleration.
items.answer: (a) Parallel, equally spaced, pointing vertically downwards (uniform). (b) 1.84 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) parallel/equally spaced [1]; downwards [1] [2] (b) a = (F − mg)/m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.84 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the SI unit of gravitational field strength?
items.answer: N kg⁻¹
items.markingKey: g = F/m: N kg⁻¹ (equivalent to m s⁻²).

items.stem: Explain why gravitational field lines never cross.
items.answer: A field line shows the direction of the force on a mass at that point; if lines crossed, the force would have two directions at one point, which is impossible.
items.markingKey: line gives direction of force [1]; unique direction at each point [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between the mass and the weight of an astronaut, and explain which changes on a journey to Mars.
items.answer: Mass is the amount of matter (resistance to acceleration) and is constant; weight is the gravitational force mg and depends on the local field strength, so weight changes.
items.markingKey: mass constant [1]; weight = mg, changes with g [1] [2]

items.stem: The gravitational field strength at the surface of Earth is 9.81 N kg⁻¹. A scientific instrument has a mass of 25 kg. What is the weight of a scientific instrument on Earth?
The gravitational field strength at the surface of Mars is 3.73 N kg⁻¹. A lander has a mass of 850 kg. Calculate the weight of a lander on Mars.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 850 × 3.73 = 3170 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A sample container has a weight of 1690 N on the surface of Neptune, where it has mass 150 kg. Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Neptune and the weight of the same object on Earth.

A lander of mass 500 kg rests on the surface of Mercury, where the gravitational field strength is 3.70 N kg⁻¹. (a) Calculate the weight of the lander. (b) The lander's thrusters give an upward force of 2770 N on lift-off. Calculate its initial acceleration.
items.markingKey: (a) W = mg (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1850 N with unit [1] [2] (b) a = (F − mg)/m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.84 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Two point masses attract each other with force F. The distance between them is doubled. What is the new force?
items.markingKey: F ∝ 1/r².

items.stem: Derive the expression g = GM/r² for the field strength due to a point mass M.
items.answer: Force on test mass m: F = GMm/r²; g = F/m = GM/r².
items.markingKey: F = GMm/r² [1]; divide by m [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the gravitational force between two students sitting next to each other is not noticed.
items.answer: G is very small (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²); for masses of about 60 kg at 1 m the force is about 10⁻⁷ N, negligible compared with friction and their weights.
items.markingKey: G very small [1]; force ~10⁻⁷ N, negligible compared to other forces [1] [2]

items.stem: The centres of the Sun (mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) and the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) are 1.50 × 10¹¹ m apart. Work out the gravitational force between them.
items.markingKey: F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.99 × 10³⁰ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/(1.50 × 10¹¹)² = 3.52 × 10²² N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The centres of the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) and the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg) are 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart. Work out the gravitational force between them.
items.markingKey: F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 5.97 × 10²⁴ × 7.35 × 10²²/(3.84 × 10⁸)² = 1.98 × 10²⁰ N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [3]

items.stem: The centres of the Sun (mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) and the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) are 1.50 × 10¹¹ m apart. (a) Calculate the gravitational force between them. (b) Calculate the separation at which the force would be one ninth of this value.

Jupiter may be treated as a uniform sphere of radius 6.99 × 10⁷ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 25.9 N kg⁻¹. (a) Show that the mass of Jupiter is about 1.9 × 10²⁷ kg. (b) Calculate the field strength at a distance of 3R from the centre.
items.answer: (a) M = gR²/G = 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg (b) 2.88 N kg⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) g = GM/R² [1]; substitution and answer [1] [2] (b) g ∝ 1/r², ÷ 9 (method/substitution) [1]; answer 2.88 N kg⁻¹ with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: The Moon may be treated as a uniform sphere of radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 1.62 N kg⁻¹. (a) Show that the mass of the Moon is about 7.4 × 10²² kg. (b) Explain why the planet can be treated as a point mass for points outside it. (c) Sketch-describe how g varies with distance r from the centre for r > R.
items.answer: (a) M = gR²/G = 7.35 × 10²² kg (b) For a uniform sphere the field outside is the same as if all its mass were at its centre. (c) g decreases as 1/r²: a curve falling steeply then levelling towards zero, never reaching it.
items.markingKey: (a) g = GM/R² [1]; substitution and answer [1] [2] (b) For a uniform sphere the field outside is the same as if all its mass were at its centre [1] (c) decreasing curve [1]; inverse square / asymptotic to zero [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the unit of the gravitational constant G?
items.answer: N m² kg⁻²
items.markingKey: G = Fr²/(Mm).

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) State Newton's law of gravitation. (b) Planet P has twice the mass and twice the radius of planet Q. The surface field strength on P compared with Q is …
items.answer: (a) Two point masses attract each other with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of their separation. (b) half as large
items.markingKey: (a) force ∝ product of masses [1]; ∝ 1/separation² (point masses) [1] [2] (b) g = GM/R² ∝ 2/4.

items.stem: Explain why the value of g measured at the top of a high mountain is slightly smaller than at sea level.
items.answer: g = GM/r²; at the top the distance from the Earth's centre is greater, so g is smaller.
items.markingKey: g ∝ 1/r² [1]; r larger at summit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the gravitational force on a satellite does not fall to zero even though it is a long way from Earth.
items.answer: The force is inversely proportional to r², so it decreases with distance but only becomes zero at infinite separation.
items.markingKey: inverse square law [1]; zero only at infinity [1] [2]

items.stem: Venus has mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m. Calculate the gravitational field strength at the surface of Venus.
items.answer: 8.87 N kg⁻¹
items.markingKey: g = GM/R² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.87 × 10²⁴/(6.05 × 10⁶)² = 8.87 N kg⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The centres of Jupiter (mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg) and its moon Io (mass 8.93 × 10²² kg) are 4.22 × 10⁸ m apart. Work out the gravitational force between them.
items.markingKey: F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.90 × 10²⁷ × 8.93 × 10²²/(4.22 × 10⁸)² = 6.35 × 10²² N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Jupiter has mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg and radius 6.99 × 10⁷ m. Calculate the gravitational field strength at a height of 3.50 × 10⁷ m above the surface.
items.answer: 11.5 N kg⁻¹

items.stem: Mercury may be treated as a uniform sphere of radius 2.44 × 10⁶ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 3.70 N kg⁻¹. (a) State Newton's law of gravitation. (b) Show that the mass of Mercury is about 3.3 × 10²³ kg. (c) Explain why the planet can be treated as a point mass for points outside it.
items.answer: (a) Force between point masses ∝ product of masses and ∝ 1/separation². (b) M = gR²/G = 3.30 × 10²³ kg (c) For a uniform sphere the field outside is the same as if all its mass were at its centre.
items.markingKey: (a) product of masses [1]; inverse square of separation [1] [2] (b) g = GM/R² [1]; substitution and answer [1] [2] (c) For a uniform sphere the field outside is the same as if all its mass were at its centre [1]

items.stem: The Moon may be treated as a uniform sphere of radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 1.62 N kg⁻¹. (a) State Newton's law of gravitation. (b) Show that the mass of the Moon is about 7.4 × 10²² kg. (c) Sketch-describe how g varies with distance r from the centre for r > R.
items.answer: (a) Force between point masses ∝ product of masses and ∝ 1/separation². (b) M = gR²/G = 7.35 × 10²² kg (c) g decreases as 1/r²: a curve falling steeply then levelling towards zero, never reaching it.
items.markingKey: (a) product of masses [1]; inverse square of separation [1] [2] (b) g = GM/R² [1]; substitution and answer [1] [2] (c) decreasing curve [1]; inverse square / asymptotic to zero [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the definition of gravitational potential at a point?
options: the work done in moving a mass from the point to the surface
the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point
the force per unit mass at the point
the energy per unit mass needed to orbit at the point
items.answer: the work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point
items.markingKey: φ = −GM/r; zero at infinity.

items.stem: Explain why the equation ΔEp = mgΔh can be used near the Earth's surface but not for a rocket travelling to a high orbit.
items.answer: mgΔh assumes g is constant (uniform field); for large changes in height g decreases significantly, so ΔEp = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) must be used.
items.markingKey: mgΔh assumes uniform g [1]; g varies over large distances, use −GMm/r [1] [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between gravitational potential and gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: Potential is the work done per unit mass bringing a test mass from infinity (a property of the point, J kg⁻¹); potential energy is the work done for a particular mass m (J), Ep = mφ.
items.markingKey: potential: per unit mass, property of the point [1]; PE: for a particular mass, Ep = mφ [1] [2]

items.stem: Venus has mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m. Determine the gravitational potential at the surface of Venus.
items.markingKey: φ = −GM/R = −6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 4.87 × 10²⁴/6.05 × 10⁶ = −5.37 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: Mercury has mass 3.30 × 10²³ kg and radius 2.44 × 10⁶ m. A satellite of mass 1200 kg is raised from the surface to a height of 2.44 × 10⁶ m above it. Calculate the increase in its gravitational potential energy.

Mercury has mass 3.30 × 10²³ kg and radius 2.44 × 10⁶ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational potential at the surface. (b) Calculate the escape speed from the surface. (c) Calculate the change in potential energy of a 250 kg probe moved from the surface to a distance 3.0R from the centre.
Venus has mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg and radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m. (a) Define gravitational potential at a point. (b) Calculate the escape speed from the surface.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point. (b) 1.04 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) work done per unit mass [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) ½v² = GM/R (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.04 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Jupiter has mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg and radius 6.99 × 10⁷ m. (a) Define gravitational potential at a point. (b) Calculate the gravitational potential at the surface. (c) Calculate the potential at a height R above the surface.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point. (b) −1.81 × 10⁹ J kg⁻¹ (c) −9.07 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) work done per unit mass [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) φ = −GM/R (method/substitution) [1]; answer −1.81 × 10⁹ J kg⁻¹ [1] [2] (c) φ ∝ 1/r, r = 2R: −9.07 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹ [1]

items.stem: Why is gravitational potential always negative?
options: Because potential energy is a vector
The potential is zero at infinity and work is done by the field as a mass moves in from infinity
items.answer: The potential is zero at infinity and work is done by the field as a mass moves in from infinity
items.markingKey: Gravity is attractive, so energy is released bringing a mass closer; potential decreases from zero.

items.stem: Explain, in terms of energy, the condition for a projectile to escape from the gravitational field of a planet.
items.answer: Its kinetic energy at launch must be at least equal to the work needed to move it to infinity, ½mv² ≥ GMm/R, so its total energy is at least zero.
items.markingKey: KE ≥ GMm/R [1]; reaches infinity with KE ≥ 0 / total energy ≥ 0 [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the gravitational potential energy of a satellite increases when it moves to a higher orbit, although the magnitude of GMm/r decreases.
items.answer: Ep = −GMm/r; increasing r makes Ep less negative, i.e. larger; work must be done against gravity to raise it.
items.markingKey: Ep negative [1]; less negative = increase [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the gravitational potential energy of a satellite increases when it moves to a higher orbit, although the magnitude of GMm/r decreases. (b) Explain why the equation ΔEp = mgΔh can be used near the Earth's surface but not for a rocket travelling to a high orbit.
items.answer: (a) Ep = −GMm/r; increasing r makes Ep less negative, i.e. larger; work must be done against gravity to raise it. (b) mgΔh assumes g is constant (uniform field); for large changes in height g decreases significantly, so ΔEp = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) must be used.
items.markingKey: (a) Ep negative [1]; less negative = increase [1] [2] (b) mgΔh assumes uniform g [1]; g varies over large distances, use −GMm/r [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain, in terms of energy, the condition for a projectile to escape from the gravitational field of a planet. (b) Distinguish between gravitational potential and gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: (a) Its kinetic energy at launch must be at least equal to the work needed to move it to infinity, ½mv² ≥ GMm/R, so its total energy is at least zero. (b) Potential is the work done per unit mass bringing a test mass from infinity (a property of the point, J kg⁻¹); potential energy is the work done for a particular mass m (J), Ep = mφ.
items.markingKey: (a) KE ≥ GMm/R [1]; reaches infinity with KE ≥ 0 / total energy ≥ 0 [1] [2] (b) potential: per unit mass, property of the point [1]; PE: for a particular mass, Ep = mφ [1] [2]

items.stem: A meteoroid is at rest relative to Mars (mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg, radius 3.39 × 10⁶ m) at a height of 1.70 × 10⁶ m above its surface. It falls towards Mars. Ignoring any atmosphere, calculate its speed on reaching the surface.
items.markingKey: loss of PE = gain of KE: ½v² = GM(1/R − 1/r) [1]; r = 5.08 × 10⁶ m [1]; v = 2.90 × 10³ m s⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: Mars has mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg and radius 3.39 × 10⁶ m. Calculate the gravitational potential at the surface of Mars.
items.markingKey: φ = −GM/R = −6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 6.42 × 10²³/3.39 × 10⁶ = −1.26 × 10⁷ J kg⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The Moon has mass 7.35 × 10²² kg and radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m. (a) Define gravitational potential at a point. (b) Calculate the minimum energy needed to move a 1.0 kg mass from the surface to infinity.
items.answer: (a) Work done per unit mass in bringing a small test mass from infinity to the point. (b) 2.82 × 10⁶ J
items.markingKey: (a) work done per unit mass [1]; from infinity [1] [2] (b) ΔE = 0 − φ: 2.82 × 10⁶ J [1]

items.stem: Mercury has mass 3.30 × 10²³ kg and radius 2.44 × 10⁶ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational potential at the surface. (b) Calculate the potential at a height R above the surface. (c) Calculate the escape speed from the surface. (d) Explain why the potential is negative.
items.answer: (a) −9.02 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ (b) −4.51 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ (c) 4.25 × 10³ m s⁻¹ (d) Zero at infinity; attractive field does work as mass moves in, so potential is below zero.
items.markingKey: (a) φ = −GM/R (method/substitution) [1]; answer −9.02 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) φ ∝ 1/r, r = 2R: −4.51 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹ [1] (c) ½v² = GM/R (method/substitution) [1]; answer 4.25 × 10³ m s⁻¹ [1] [2] (d) Zero at infinity; attractive field does work as mass moves in, so potential is below zero [1]

items.stem: Which is a property of a geostationary satellite?
options: It orbits over the poles every 24 hours
It can be placed at any height above any point
It orbits above the equator with a period of 24 hours
It is stationary relative to the Sun
items.answer: It orbits above the equator with a period of 24 hours
items.markingKey: It stays above one point: equatorial, west to east, T = 24 h.

items.stem: Show that for a satellite in a circular orbit T² = (4π²/GM) r³.
items.answer: GMm/r² = mω²r with ω = 2π/T: GM/r² = 4π²r/T², so T² = 4π²r³/(GM).
items.markingKey: gravitational force = centripetal force [1]; ω = 2π/T and rearrange [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a geostationary satellite must be above the equator.
items.answer: The centripetal force (gravity) is directed towards the Earth's centre, so the orbit must be centred on the centre; to stay above one point while the Earth rotates, the orbit must lie in the equatorial plane.
items.markingKey: orbit centred on Earth's centre [1]; only equatorial orbit stays above a fixed point [1] [2]

items.stem: A satellite orbits Mars (mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg, radius 3.39 × 10⁶ m) in a circular orbit at a height of 1.36 × 10⁷ m above the surface. Work out the orbital speed.
items.markingKey: v = √(GM/r), r = 1.70 × 10⁷ m = 1590 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A satellite orbits Venus (mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m) in a circular orbit at a height of 3.02 × 10⁶ m above the surface. Calculate the orbital speed and the period of the orbit.

A satellite of mass 450 kg is in a circular orbit 2.00 × 10⁷ m above the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m). (a) Show that the orbital speed is given by v = √(GM/r). (b) Calculate the period in hours.
items.answer: (a) GMm/r² = mv²/r, so v² = GM/r. (b) 11.8 h
items.markingKey: (a) equate gravitational and centripetal force [1]; rearrange [1] [2] (b) T = 2πr/v (method/substitution) [1]; answer 11.8 h with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: For satellites in circular orbits around the same planet, the square of the period T is proportional to …
items.answer: r³
items.markingKey: GMm/r² = mω²r ⇒ T² = 4π²r³/(GM).

items.stem: Explain why astronauts in an orbiting space station feel weightless although gravity acts on them.
items.answer: They and the station are both in free fall with the same acceleration towards the Earth; there is no contact force between astronaut and floor, which is what is sensed as weight.
items.markingKey: both in free fall / same acceleration [1]; no normal contact force [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the orbital speed of a satellite does not depend on its mass.
items.answer: GMm/r² = mv²/r; m cancels, so v = √(GM/r) depends only on M and r.
items.markingKey: equate forces [1]; m cancels [1] [2]

items.stem: A satellite orbits Neptune (mass 1.02 × 10²⁶ kg, radius 2.46 × 10⁷ m) in a circular orbit at a height of 2.46 × 10⁷ m above the surface. What is the orbital speed?
Mars has mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg and rotates once every 88 600 s. Calculate the radius of the orbit of a synchronous satellite of Mars.
items.markingKey: GMm/r² = m(2π/T)²r [1]; r³ = GMT²/4π² [1]; r = 2.04 × 10⁷ m [1] [3]

items.stem: The Earth orbits the Sun in a near-circular orbit of radius 1.50 × 10¹¹ m with a period of 3.16 × 10⁷ s. Determine the mass of the Sun.
items.markingKey: GMm/r² = m(4π²/T²)r [1]; M = 4π²r³/(GT²) [1]; = 2.00 × 10³⁰ kg [1] [3]

items.stem: A satellite of mass 1200 kg is in a circular orbit 2.00 × 10⁷ m above the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m). (a) Calculate the orbital speed. (b) Calculate the period in hours.
items.markingKey: (a) r = R + h, v = √(GM/r) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 3890 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) T = 2πr/v (method/substitution) [1]; answer 11.8 h with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Which describes the gravitational field lines around an isolated spherical planet?
options: radial and directed away from the centre
radial and directed towards the centre
items.answer: radial and directed towards the centre
items.markingKey: Field lines show the direction of the force on a mass: inwards, radial.

items.stem: Describe the pattern of gravitational field lines for the field around an isolated planet, and explain what the pattern shows about the field strength.
items.answer: Radial lines pointing inwards towards the centre, getting further apart with distance; the closer the lines, the stronger the field.
items.markingKey: correct shape and direction [1]; spacing related to field strength [1] ; reason linked to inverse-square law or uniformity [1] [3]

items.stem: Two bodies of masses 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg and 7.35 × 10²² kg have centres 3.84 × 10⁸ m apart. Calculate the distance from the centre of the larger body to the point on the line between them where the resultant gravitational field strength is zero.

Earth may be treated as a uniform sphere of radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m. The gravitational field strength at its surface is 9.81 N kg⁻¹. (a) State Newton's law of gravitation. (b) Show that the mass of Earth is about 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. (c) Explain why the planet can be treated as a point mass for points outside it.
items.answer: (a) Force between point masses ∝ product of masses and ∝ 1/separation². (b) M = gR²/G = 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg (c) For a uniform sphere the field outside is the same as if all its mass were at its centre.
items.markingKey: (a) product of masses [1]; inverse square of separation [1] [2] (b) g = GM/R² [1]; substitution and answer [1] [2] (c) For a uniform sphere the field outside is the same as if all its mass were at its centre [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) The gravitational potential at distance r from a planet is φ. What is it at distance 2r? (b) What is the unit of gravitational potential?
items.answer: (a) φ/2 (b) J kg⁻¹
items.markingKey: (a) φ ∝ −1/r. (b) Work per unit mass.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain, in terms of energy, the condition for a projectile to escape from the gravitational field of a planet. (b) Explain why the equation ΔEp = mgΔh can be used near the Earth's surface but not for a rocket travelling to a high orbit.
items.answer: (a) Its kinetic energy at launch must be at least equal to the work needed to move it to infinity, ½mv² ≥ GMm/R, so its total energy is at least zero. (b) mgΔh assumes g is constant (uniform field); for large changes in height g decreases significantly, so ΔEp = GMm(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) must be used.
items.markingKey: (a) KE ≥ GMm/R [1]; reaches infinity with KE ≥ 0 / total energy ≥ 0 [1] [2] (b) mgΔh assumes uniform g [1]; g varies over large distances, use −GMm/r [1] [2]

items.stem: A meteoroid is at rest relative to Mercury (mass 3.30 × 10²³ kg, radius 2.44 × 10⁶ m) at a height of 4.88 × 10⁶ m above its surface. It falls towards Mercury. Ignoring any atmosphere, calculate its speed on reaching the surface.
items.markingKey: loss of PE = gain of KE: ½v² = GM(1/R − 1/r) [1]; r = 7.32 × 10⁶ m [1]; v = 3.47 × 10³ m s⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: Mercury has mass 3.30 × 10²³ kg and radius 2.44 × 10⁶ m. Work out the gravitational potential at the surface of Mercury.
items.markingKey: φ = −GM/R = −6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 3.30 × 10²³/2.44 × 10⁶ = −9.02 × 10⁶ J kg⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A meteoroid is at rest relative to Venus (mass 4.87 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.05 × 10⁶ m) at a height of 1.21 × 10⁷ m above its surface. It falls towards Venus. Ignoring any atmosphere, calculate its speed on reaching the surface.
items.markingKey: loss of PE = gain of KE: ½v² = GM(1/R − 1/r) [1]; r = 1.81 × 10⁷ m [1]; v = 8.46 × 10³ m s⁻¹ [1] [3]

items.stem: Jupiter has mass 1.90 × 10²⁷ kg and radius 6.99 × 10⁷ m. (a) Calculate the gravitational potential at the surface. (b) Calculate the potential at a height R above the surface. (c) Calculate the minimum energy needed to move a 1.0 kg mass from the surface to infinity. (d) Calculate the escape speed from the surface.
items.markingKey: (a) φ = −GM/R (method/substitution) [1]; answer −1.81 × 10⁹ J kg⁻¹ [1] [2] (b) φ ∝ 1/r, r = 2R: −9.07 × 10⁸ J kg⁻¹ [1] (c) ΔE = 0 − φ: 1.81 × 10⁹ J [1] (d) ½v² = GM/R (method/substitution) [1]; answer 6.02 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ [1] [2]

items.stem: Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of geostationary satellites for communications.
items.answer: Advantage: stays above one point so dishes need no tracking / continuous coverage. Disadvantage: very high orbit gives a time delay and needs powerful signals; poor coverage near the poles.
items.markingKey: advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Show that for a satellite in a circular orbit T² = (4π²/GM) r³. (b) Suggest one advantage and one disadvantage of geostationary satellites for communications.
items.answer: (a) GMm/r² = mω²r with ω = 2π/T: GM/r² = 4π²r/T², so T² = 4π²r³/(GM). (b) Advantage: stays above one point so dishes need no tracking / continuous coverage. Disadvantage: very high orbit gives a time delay and needs powerful signals; poor coverage near the poles.
items.markingKey: (a) gravitational force = centripetal force [1]; ω = 2π/T and rearrange [1] [2] (b) advantage [1]; disadvantage [1] [2]

items.stem: A satellite orbits the Moon (mass 7.35 × 10²² kg, radius 1.74 × 10⁶ m) in a circular orbit at a height of 6.96 × 10⁶ m above the surface. Calculate the orbital speed.
items.answer: 751 m s⁻¹
items.markingKey: v = √(GM/r), r = 8.70 × 10⁶ m = 751 m s⁻¹. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A satellite of mass 800 kg is in a circular orbit 8.00 × 10⁵ m above the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg, radius 6.37 × 10⁶ m). (a) Calculate the orbital speed. (b) Calculate the period in hours.
items.markingKey: (a) r = R + h, v = √(GM/r) (method/substitution) [1]; answer 7450 m s⁻¹ with unit [1] [2] (b) T = 2πr/v (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.68 h with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Close to the Earth's surface, over a small region, the gravitational field is …
items.answer: approximately uniform
items.markingKey: Field lines are nearly parallel and equally spaced over a small height range.

items.stem: Describe the pattern of gravitational field lines for the field between the Earth and the Moon along the line joining them, and explain what the pattern shows about the field strength.
items.answer: Lines pointing towards each body, with a point between them (closer to the Moon) where the resultant field is zero; the closer the lines, the stronger the field.
items.markingKey: correct shape and direction [1]; spacing related to field strength [1] ; reason linked to inverse-square law or uniformity [1] [3]

items.stem: The gravitational field strength at the surface of Neptune is 11.2 N kg⁻¹. A rover has a mass of 60 kg. Calculate the weight of a rover on Neptune.
items.markingKey: W = mg = 60 × 11.2 = 675 N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: A lander of mass 500 kg rests on the surface of Mercury, where the gravitational field strength is 3.70 N kg⁻¹. (a) Describe the field lines close to the surface over the landing site. (b) The lander's thrusters give an upward force of 2770 N on lift-off. Calculate its initial acceleration.
items.answer: (a) Parallel, equally spaced, pointing vertically downwards (uniform). (b) 1.84 m s⁻²
items.markingKey: (a) parallel/equally spaced [1]; downwards [1] [2] (b) a = (F − mg)/m (method/substitution) [1]; answer 1.84 m s⁻² with unit [1] [2]

items.stem: Planet P has twice the mass and twice the radius of planet Q. The surface field strength on P compared with Q is …
items.answer: half as large
items.markingKey: g = GM/R² ∝ 2/4.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Derive the expression g = GM/r² for the field strength due to a point mass M. (b) Explain why the value of g measured at the top of a high mountain is slightly smaller than at sea level.
items.answer: (a) Force on test mass m: F = GMm/r²; g = F/m = GM/r². (b) g = GM/r²; at the top the distance from the Earth's centre is greater, so g is smaller.
items.markingKey: (a) F = GMm/r² [1]; divide by m [1] [2] (b) g ∝ 1/r² [1]; r larger at summit [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the gravitational force between two students sitting next to each other is not noticed. (b) Explain why the gravitational force on a satellite does not fall to zero even though it is a long way from Earth.
items.answer: (a) G is very small (6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²); for masses of about 60 kg at 1 m the force is about 10⁻⁷ N, negligible compared with friction and their weights. (b) The force is inversely proportional to r², so it decreases with distance but only becomes zero at infinite separation.
items.markingKey: (a) G very small [1]; force ~10⁻⁷ N, negligible compared to other forces [1] [2] (b) inverse square law [1]; zero only at infinity [1] [2]

items.stem: The centres of the Sun (mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) and the Earth (mass 5.97 × 10²⁴ kg) are 1.50 × 10¹¹ m apart. Calculate the gravitational force between them.
items.markingKey: F = GMm/r² = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.99 × 10³⁰ × 5.97 × 10²⁴/(1.50 × 10¹¹)² = 3.52 × 10²² N. (equation/substitution, then answer with unit) [2]

items.stem: The centres of the Sun (mass 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg) and Mars (mass 6.42 × 10²³ kg) are 2.28 × 10¹¹ m apart. Work out the gravitational force between them.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why the gravitational potential energy of a satellite increases when it moves to a higher orbit, although the magnitude of GMm/r decreases. (b) Distinguish between gravitational potential and gravitational potential energy.
items.answer: (a) Ep = −GMm/r; increasing r makes Ep less negative, i.e. larger; work must be done against gravity to raise it. (b) Potential is the work done per unit mass bringing a test mass from infinity (a property of the point, J kg⁻¹); potential energy is the work done for a particular mass m (J), Ep = mφ.
items.markingKey: (a) Ep negative [1]; less negative = increase [1] [2] (b) potential: per unit mass, property of the point [1]; PE: for a particular mass, Ep = mφ [1] [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why astronauts in an orbiting space station feel weightless although gravity acts on them. (b) Explain why a geostationary satellite must be above the equator.
items.answer: (a) They and the station are both in free fall with the same acceleration towards the Earth; there is no contact force between astronaut and floor, which is what is sensed as weight. (b) The centripetal force (gravity) is directed towards the Earth's centre, so the orbit must be centred on the centre; to stay above one point while the Earth rotates, the orbit must lie in the equatorial plane.
items.markingKey: (a) both in free fall / same acceleration [1]; no normal contact force [1] [2] (b) orbit centred on Earth's centre [1]; only equatorial orbit stays above a fixed point [1] [2]
